briefs.pyelo:
Pyelonephritis

home or admit · imaging gates · organism from the urine · complicated vs uncomplicatedCan the patient take oral therapy safely, and what does the urine say about the organism?

DiagnosisManagementPractice
Bottom line

Fever, chills, dysuria and costovertebral angle tenderness make pyelonephritis a clinical diagnosis; with a benign abdomen, treat without imaging.

Admit for intravenous (IV) antibiotics when any of these holds:

  • Cannot take oral therapy: vomiting, or only clear fluids for days.
  • Unstable: sepsis or hypotension, read against the baseline (104/68 is low in long-standing hypertension).
  • Anatomy or host: pregnancy, obstruction, stones or a catheter; immunocompromise or extremes of age.
  • Failed outpatient therapy, or no oral agent the organism is sensitive to.

Otherwise a healthy, stable patient tolerating oral intake goes home on oral therapy. Nitrofurantoin treats cystitis, not the kidney.

Diagnosis
Defining criteria Pyelonephritis – fever and chills with flank or costovertebral angle tenderness and urinary symptoms · Complicated UTI (urinary tract infection) – infection beyond the bladder: systemic signs such as fever or bacteremia, a catheter-related infection, or pyelonephritis (IDSA (Infectious Diseases Society of America) 2025); men can have uncomplicated cystitis. Older teaching called every UTI in a man complicated ⚠︎ · Duration – every pyelonephritis is a complicated UTI: typically 7 days, oral or IV, switching to oral as soon as the patient improves (IDSA 2025; older teaching 7 to 14 days ⚠︎)
Which enzyme Nitrate reductase – nitrate to nitrite: Escherichia coli, Klebsiella, Proteus, Enterobacter; not Staphylococcus saprophyticus, Enterococcus or Pseudomonas · Urease – urea to ammonia, alkaline urine, struvite staghorn stones: Proteus, Klebsiella, S. saprophyticus · Catheter, instrumentation, prior antibiotics or hospital – Enterococcus and Pseudomonas (nitrite-negative), Citrobacter, Serratia, Enterobacter; the stem supplies the exposure
Management and treatment
Management ladder: pyelonephritis
TierInterventionEscalate when
OutpatientOral therapy chosen by local resistance: in adults, a fluoroquinolone, or trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX) if the organism is sensitive; in a well child, an oral third-generation cephalosporin; avoid fluoroquinolones in childrenAny admission criterion, or failure of outpatient therapy
AdmitIV antibiotics; switch to oral as soon as the patient improvesNo improvement at 48 to 72 hours: CT for abscess or obstruction
Source controlDrain an abscess or relieve an obstruction; urgent urology for emphysematous pyelonephritisTop rung
By diagnosis Cystitis – no fever, no flank tenderness: nitrofurantoin · Pyelonephritis in pregnancy – admit for IV antibiotics · Benign prostatic hyperplasia – incomplete emptying causes stasis and ascending infection · Struvite stones – a urease organism, usually Proteus
Practice
  1. 28-year-old woman has 2 days of fever, chills and dysuria right costovertebral angle tenderness eating and drinking normally Healthy; not pregnant T 38.6 °C · BP 118/74 mm Hg · HR 96/min · abdomen benign → Outpatient oral therapy → a healthy, stable patient who tolerates oral intake is treated at home with oral therapy; nitrofurantoin does not reach the kidney
  2. 28-year-old woman has fever, flank pain and dysuria has taken only clear fluids for 2 days vomits everything, including her tablets Healthy; not pregnant T 39.0 °C · BP 110/70 mm Hg · left costovertebral angle tenderness → Admit for IV antibiotics → a patient who cannot keep oral therapy down is admitted for IV antibiotics; one intramuscular dose does not finish the course
  3. 28-year-old woman at 24 weeks of gestation has fever and flank pain dysuria for 3 days right costovertebral angle tenderness Tolerating fluids; no contractions T 38.8 °C · BP 112/68 mm Hg · fetal heart rate 150/min → Admit for IV antibiotics → pregnancy is on the admission list by itself, even with oral intake intact; nitrofurantoin does not treat the kidney
  4. 28-year-old woman has 2 days of dysuria and frequency suprapubic discomfort no flank pain or costovertebral angle tenderness Not pregnant; no vaginal discharge Afebrile · BP 116/72 mm Hg · urinalysis: nitrites positive → Treat as cystitis with nitrofurantoin → no fever and no flank tenderness is cystitis: nitrofurantoin; it does not treat pyelonephritis; a fluoroquinolone is not first line for cystitis, and 14 days is a pyelonephritis-length course
  5. 28-year-old woman admitted with fever and flank pain is still febrile 72 hours of IV antibiotics matched to the culture flank pain unchanged Blood cultures negative T 39.1 °C · BP 108/70 mm Hg · creatinine 1.0 mg/dL → CT for abscess or obstruction → no improvement at 48 to 72 hours on correct antibiotics: CT for an abscess or obstruction, not broader antibiotics
  6. 28-year-old woman has fever, flank pain and dysuria eating and drinking a past culture grew an organism resistant to every oral agent Not pregnant T 38.7 °C · BP 120/76 mm Hg · left costovertebral angle tenderness → Admit for IV therapy → no oral option means IV therapy, so she is admitted; nitrofurantoin does not reach the kidney
  7. 9-month-old girl has 2 days of fever and fussiness feeding poorly but still drinking well no cough, rash or diarrhea Catheterized urine culture sent; no drug allergies T 39.0 °C · urinalysis: nitrites positive, leukocyte esterase positive → Cefixime → a third-generation cephalosporin such as cefixime covers the gram-negative uropathogens; ciprofloxacin is avoided in children, and clindamycin misses them
  8. 11-month-old boy has a first febrile urinary infection well-appearing, taking fluids pediatrician prescribes cefixime, not trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole or amoxicillin-clavulanate Parents ask why the two older drugs were not used T 38.9 °C · urinalysis: nitrites positive → Rising Escherichia coli resistance → rising Escherichia coli resistance; the local resistance pattern drives the empiric choice
  9. 9-month-old girl has a first febrile urinary infection well-appearing, tolerating oral intake culture sensitivities pending No drug allergies; parents ask which drugs are options T 38.8 °C · urinalysis: nitrites positive, leukocyte esterase positive → Ciprofloxacin → fluoroquinolones are avoided in children (cartilage toxicity) and kept for organisms such as Pseudomonas with no alternative; an oral cephalosporin fits
  10. 72-year-old man with an indwelling urinary catheter has fever right flank pain catheter in place for 6 weeks Several antibiotic courses this year T 38.9 °C · BP 128/80 mm Hg · urinalysis: nitrites negative, pyuria → Pseudomonas aeruginosa → a catheter, instrumentation or prior antibiotics widen the organism list beyond Escherichia coli to Pseudomonas, Enterococcus, Serratia and Candida
  11. 58-year-old woman has a third urinary infection this year urine pH 8.5 on every recent urinalysis CT: staghorn calculus filling the left renal pelvis No catheter Afebrile · BP 124/80 mm Hg · urinalysis: nitrites positive → Proteus mirabilis → urease splits urea to ammonia, alkalinizes the urine and builds struvite staghorn stones: Proteus mirabilis; Klebsiella also has urease but is a far less common cause
  12. 22-year-old woman has 2 days of dysuria and frequency sexually active, with a new partner this month culture: gram-positive cocci, coagulase-negative, novobiocin-resistant No flank pain Afebrile · urinalysis: leukocyte esterase positive, nitrites negative → Staphylococcus saprophyticus → Staphylococcus saprophyticus: young sexually active women, coagulase-negative, novobiocin-resistant, and nitrite-negative because it lacks nitrate reductase
  13. 26-year-old woman has 1 week of dysuria sexually active, inconsistent condom use pyuria, but the urine culture is sterile No flank pain Afebrile · BP 114/70 mm Hg · urinalysis: nitrites negative → Chlamydial urethritis → sterile pyuria in a sexually active patient is chlamydial urethritis until shown otherwise: nucleic acid amplification test (NAAT)
  14. 64-year-old man with poorly controlled diabetes has fever and flank pain worse despite 2 days of antibiotics CT: gas within the left renal parenchyma Glucose 420 mg/dL T 39.4 °C · BP 96/60 mm Hg · HR 118/min → Emphysematous pyelonephritis → gas in the kidney of a diabetic is emphysematous pyelonephritis: IV antibiotics, glucose control and urgent urology
  15. 45-year-old man has his fourth urinary infection in 2 years every culture grows Proteus mirabilis urine pH 8.0 Imaging shows a large branching calculus in the right renal pelvis Afebrile · BP 126/82 mm Hg → Struvite stones → a urease-splitting organism alkalinizes the urine and precipitates struvite (magnesium ammonium phosphate)
Pairs with Urinary Tract Infection in a Child covers febrile infection in children, the imaging that follows it and afebrile recurrences. Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia and Urinary Retention covers the obstruction behind infection in an older man. Ask: is the infection in the bladder or beyond it?
Transferable rule

Treat a clinical diagnosis without imaging, and image only for a named reason. When an organism is ruled out by an enzyme, name the enzyme: urease and nitrate reductase are independent.
